b: In 1970, roboticist Masahiro Mori proposed that as robots look more human we like them more, until they become almost but not quite human. Then they turn creepy. He called that dip the uncanny valley.

q.p: Why might a very lifelike robot feel creepy?
o: It's almost but not quite human

why: Small flaws in near-human faces may signal something is wrong.

b: If every plank of a ship is replaced one by one, is it still the same ship? And if you rebuilt the old planks into a second ship, which is the original? Plutarch recorded the puzzle nearly 2,000 years ago, and it still fuels debates about identity.

q.p: What does the Ship of Theseus puzzle ask about?
o: Whether something stays the same if all its parts change

why: Your body's cells are also replaced over time.

b: Occam's razor, named after the 14th-century friar William of Ockham, advises: don't add more assumptions than you need. When two explanations fit the facts equally well, prefer the simpler one. It's a guide, not a proof.

q.p: What does Occam's razor suggest?

o: No, it's a rule of thumb

why: Each extra assumption is another chance to be wrong.

b: Hanlon's razor says: never attribute to malice what can be adequately explained by carelessness or mistake. It's a reminder that most frustrating situations come from people being busy or wrong, not plotting against you.

q.p: Hanlon's razor suggests most annoying events are due to…

rq.p: What is it a useful reminder for?

why: Assuming malice often makes conflicts worse.

b: Zeno of Elea argued that fast Achilles can never overtake a tortoise with a head start: each time he reaches where it was, it has moved on a bit. Mathematicians later resolved it: infinitely many shrinking steps can add up to a finite distance.

q.p: What resolves Zeno's Achilles paradox?
o: Infinite steps can sum to a finite distance

why: 1/2 + 1/4 + 1/8 + … adds up to exactly 1.

b: Philosopher Philippa Foot posed the trolley problem in 1967: should you divert a runaway tram to kill one person instead of five? It's used to explore the difference between doing harm and allowing it, and now informs debates about self-driving cars.

q.p: Who first posed the trolley problem?

rq.p: Which modern technology revived the debate?

why: Cars may need rules for unavoidable crash choices.

b: Socrates, one of the founders of Western philosophy, never wrote anything down that survives. We know his ideas mainly through his students, especially Plato, whose dialogues star Socrates as the main speaker.

q.p: How do we know what Socrates thought?

rq.p: Which student wrote dialogues starring Socrates?

why: Socrates preferred live conversation to writing.

b: René Descartes wanted one belief he couldn't doubt. Even if he doubted everything, he realised the act of doubting proved he existed. He wrote it in French in 1637 as 'je pense, donc je suis', later famous in Latin as 'cogito, ergo sum'.

q.p: What couldn't Descartes doubt?
o: That he existed, since he was thinking

rq.p: In which language did Descartes first publish the phrase?

why: Doubting is itself a kind of thinking.

t: Stoics split what you can control
b: The Stoic teacher Epictetus, a former slave, taught that some things are up to us, like our judgements and actions, and some aren't, like weather or others' opinions. Focusing only on the first brings peace of mind.

q.p: What did Epictetus say to focus on?

why: Worrying about uncontrollable things only adds suffering.

b: Two suspects can each stay silent or betray the other. Betrayal looks best individually, but if both betray, both do worse than if both had stayed silent. The puzzle, devised in 1950, shows how self-interest can backfire.

q.p: In the prisoner's dilemma, what happens if both betray each other?
o: Both do worse than if both stayed silent

why: Trust lets both sides reach the better outcome.

b: If a pasture is shared by everyone, each herder gains by adding one more cow, but if all do, the grass is destroyed. Ecologist Garrett Hardin popularised the idea in 1968. Economist Elinor Ostrom later showed communities often manage commons well.

q.p: Who showed communities can manage shared resources well?

rq.p: What is the 'tragedy' of the commons?
o: Individual gain ruins a shared resource

why: Ostrom won a Nobel in economics in 2009 for this work.

b: Economist Charles Goodhart noted that measures used as targets stop being good measures. Paraphrased: 'When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure.' People game the number instead of improving the real thing.

q.p: What happens when a measure becomes a target?
o: It stops being a good measure

why: Effort shifts to hitting the metric, not the goal.

b: Italian economist Vilfredo Pareto observed around 1900 that about 80% of Italy's land was owned by about 20% of the people. The 'Pareto principle' now loosely describes how a small share of causes often drives most of the effects.

q.p: What did Pareto originally observe?

why: Many real-world distributions are lopsided.

b: In the Second World War, statistician Abraham Wald studied damage on returning bombers. Rather than armouring where bullet holes clustered, he argued for armouring where returning planes had none, since planes hit there didn't come back.

q.p: Where did Wald suggest adding armour?
o: Where returning planes had no holes

rq.p: What error does survivorship bias describe?
o: Looking only at those who made it

why: The missing planes held the important information.

b: In 2003, Barbra Streisand sued to remove an aerial photo of her Malibu home from a coastal survey website. The lawsuit drew huge attention and the photo was viewed far more. Trying to hide something often spreads it.

q.p: What's the Streisand effect?
o: Trying to hide something makes it spread
An aerial photo of her home

why: Attention attracts curiosity.

b: Sitting through a terrible film because you've paid for the ticket is the sunk cost fallacy. Money or time already spent can't be recovered, so it shouldn't decide what you do next; only future costs and benefits should.

q.p: Should money already spent decide what you do next?
o: No, only future costs and benefits

rq.p: What's an example of the sunk cost fallacy?
o: Finishing a bad film because you paid

why: Past costs are gone whatever you choose.

t: We notice what we already believe
b: Confirmation bias is our tendency to seek out, remember and trust information that supports what we already think, and to brush aside what doesn't. Deliberately looking for evidence against your view helps counter it.

q.p: What is confirmation bias?
o: Favouring evidence that fits our beliefs
Look for evidence against your view

why: Agreeing evidence feels good; disagreeing evidence feels like a threat.

b: G. K. Chesterton imagined a reformer finding a fence across a road and wanting it removed. A wiser one says: first find out why it was built. Only remove a rule or tradition once you understand its purpose.

q.p: What does Chesterton's fence advise?
o: Understand why something exists before removing it

rq.p: Who came up with the idea?

why: Old rules sometimes solve problems we've forgotten.

b: In a 1955 Economist essay, historian C. Northcote Parkinson wrote that 'work expands so as to fill the time available for its completion'. Give a task a week and it tends to take a week. Tighter deadlines can help.

q.p: According to Parkinson's law, work expands to fill…

rq.p: Where was Parkinson's law first published?

why: Without a deadline, tasks absorb extra polishing and delay.

b: Douglas Hofstadter's playful law says: 'It always takes longer than you expect, even when you take into account Hofstadter's law.' It captures our persistent tendency to underestimate how long tasks take, known as the planning fallacy.

q.p: What does Hofstadter's law say?
o: Things take longer than expected, even allowing for that

why: We imagine the best case and forget surprises.

t: The map is not the territory
b: Philosopher Alfred Korzybski warned that a map, or any model, is not the reality it describes. Maps leave things out and can be out of date. The idea reminds us that our mental models are simplifications.

q.p: What does 'the map is not the territory' mean?
o: Models aren't the reality they describe

why: Every model leaves something out.

b: Mathematician Carl Jacobi advised solving hard problems by turning them around. Investor Charlie Munger made it famous: instead of asking how to succeed, ask what would guarantee failure, then avoid that.

q.p: What does 'inversion' suggest?
o: Ask what would cause failure, then avoid it

why: Mistakes are often easier to spot than perfect plans.

b: The true cost of a choice is the best thing you gave up to make it. An evening spent scrolling costs whatever else you could have done with those hours. Economists call this opportunity cost.

q.p: What is the opportunity cost of a choice?
o: The best alternative you gave up

rq.p: Spending an evening on your phone has an opportunity cost of…

why: Time and money spent on one thing can't be spent on another.

t: Starry Night was painted from an asylum
b: Vincent van Gogh painted The Starry Night in 1889 while staying at an asylum in Saint-Rémy-de-Provence in southern France. It shows the view from his window just before sunrise, with an imagined village added.

q.p: Where was Van Gogh when he painted The Starry Night?

rq.p: What part of the painting did he imagine?

why: He painted from memory and imagination as well as the view.

b: Popular images show Michelangelo lying on his back to paint the Sistine Chapel ceiling. In fact he worked standing on a scaffold he designed, painting overhead for four years, from 1508 to 1512. He wrote a poem complaining about the strain on his neck.

q.p: How did Michelangelo paint the Sistine ceiling?

rq.p: How long did the ceiling take?

why: The 'lying down' image comes from later fiction and films.
